lesson.title: Building a Financial Nation from Nothing
lesson.summary: Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury under George Washington, designed the financial system that stabilized the new nation's economy and articulated a vision of expansive federal power that shaped American politics for a generation.
lesson.body:
Alexander Hamilton's path to the center of American government was unusual from the start. Born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, he arrived in the mainland colonies as a young man, distinguished himself academically, and then served as one of George Washington's closest aides during the Revolutionary War, an experience that gave him a front-row view of just how badly the Continental Congress had struggled to fund and supply the army. That memory shaped nearly everything he did afterward, from his forceful advocacy at the Constitutional Convention to his decision, alongside James Madison and John Jay, to write the bulk of the Federalist Papers defending the Constitution's stronger national government.

When Washington appointed him the first Secretary of the Treasury in 1789, Hamilton set out to solve the debt and credit problems that had plagued the country since the Revolutionary War, problems the weak Articles of Confederation had never been able to address. In his Report on Public Credit, he proposed that the federal government assume the states' outstanding war debts and pay off the national debt at full face value, arguing that establishing the government's creditworthiness from the start was essential to attracting investment and respect from other nations. The plan was politically explosive, since it benefited states like Massachusetts that still carried heavy war debt while seeming to shortchange states like Virginia that had already paid theirs off, and it took a famous compromise, reportedly brokered over dinner with Jefferson and Madison and involving locating the new national capital along the Potomac River, to secure enough southern votes for passage.

Hamilton pushed further still, proposing the creation of the First Bank of the United States in 1791 to manage federal finances and stabilize currency, and imposing excise taxes, including the whiskey tax that would soon provoke the Whiskey Rebellion Washington personally rode out to suppress. His Report on Manufactures argued for federal support of American industry, envisioning a diversified, modern economy rather than one dependent solely on agriculture and exports.

Underlying all of this was a broader argument about the Constitution itself. Hamilton was a loose constructionist, believing the necessary and proper clause gave Congress implied powers beyond those explicitly listed, an interpretation that let him justify a national bank the Constitution never directly mentioned. Thomas Jefferson, serving alongside him in Washington's cabinet as Secretary of State, disagreed sharply, favoring a strict reading of the Constitution's limits and a more agrarian vision for the country. Their repeated clashes inside Washington's cabinet hardened into the first American party system, with Hamilton's supporters forming the Federalist Party and Jefferson's forming the Democratic-Republicans.

Hamilton never held elected office beyond his Treasury post, and his political career ended earlier than either rival's, but the financial architecture he built, and the expansive view of federal power he argued for using the same reasoning he had honed in the Federalist Papers, left a lasting mark on how the American government would operate for generations afterward.
